{{Short description|Extinct language isolate of California, US}} {{Infobox language | name = Chimariko | nativename = {{lang|cid|C'imariko}} | states = [[United States]] | region = [[California]] | ethnicity = [[Chimariko people|Chimariko]] | extinct = 1950s, with the death of Martha Ziegler | familycolor = hokan | fam1 = [[Language isolate]] or [[Hokan]] ? | dia1 = Trinity River | dia2 = South Fork | dia3 = New River | iso3 = cid | glotto = chim1301 | glottorefname = Chimariko | map = Chimariko lang.png | mapcaption = Pre-contact distribution of Chimariko | notice = IPA }} '''Chimariko''' is an [[extinct language|extinct]] [[language isolate]] formerly spoken in northern [[Trinity County, California|Trinity County]], California, by the inhabitants of several independent communities. Although the total area claimed by these communities was small, Victor Golla has argued for the recognition of three distinct local dialects: Trinity River Chimariko, spoken along the [[Trinity River (California)|Trinity River]] from the mouth of South Fork at Salyer as far upstream as Big Bar, with a principal village at [[Burnt Ranch, California|Burnt Ranch]]; South Fork Chimariko, spoken around the junction of South Fork and Hayfork Creek, with a principal village at [[Hyampom, California|Hyampom]]; and New River Chimariko, spoken along New River on the southern slopes of the [[Trinity Alps]], with a principal village at [[Denny, California|Denny]].{{Harvnb|Golla|2011|pp=87-89}} == Classification == Proposals linking Chimariko to other languages in various versions of the hypothetical Hokan family have been advanced. [[Roland Dixon]] suggested a relationship between Chimariko and the [[Shastan languages|Shastan]] and [[Palaihnihan]] families. [[Edward Sapir]]'s famous [[Classification of indigenous languages of the Americas#Sapir (1929): Encyclopædia Britannica|1929 classification]] grouped Chimariko together with the [[Shastan language|Shastan]], [[Palaihnihan languages|Palaihnihan]], [[Pomoan]], [[Karuk language|Karuk]], and [[Yana language|Yana]] languages in a [[Hokan languages|Hokan]] sub-grouping known as Northern Hokan. A "Kahi" family consisting of Chimariko, Shastan, Palaihnihan, and Karuk has been suggested. Most specialists currently find these relationships to be undemonstrated, and consider Chimariko to be best considered an isolate.{{Harvnb|Jany|2009}} ==Documentation== Stephen Powers collected the first word list from Chimariko speakers in 1875. Soon after, Jeremiah Curtin documented a substantial amount of information.{{Harvnb|Golla|2011|p=89}} Roland Dixon began work on the Chimariko language in the early 1900s, when there were few remaining speakers. Dixon worked with two: Mrs. Dyer and a man who was named Friday.{{Harvnb|Sapir|1911}} While doing work with nearby [[Hupa language|Hupa]], Edward Sapir collected data and also commented on the earlier Dixon work. Later, extensive documentation on the language was carried out by [[J.P. Harrington]], who worked with [[Sally Noble]], the last fluent speaker of the language.{{Harvnb|Luthin|2002}} None of this work has been published, but slides of all of Harrington's work can be viewed on the [[Smithsonian Institution]]'s website.{{cite web|title=John P. Harrington Papers|url=http://siris-archives.si.edu/ipac20/ipac.jsp?uri=full=3100001~!363718~!10&ri=4&aspect=basic&menu=search&source=~!siarchives&profile=all|work=National Anthropological Archives, Smithsonian Institution}} Harrington's assistant [[John Paul Marr]] also made recordings of the language with speaker Martha Ziegler.{{Cite web|url=http://collections.si.edu/search/results.jsp?view=&date.slider=&fq=online_media_type%3A%22Sound+recordings%22&fq=online_visual_material%3Atrue&q=Harrington%2C&dsort=&fq=language:%22Chimariko%22|title=Chimariko Sound recording n.d|work=collections.si.edu|access-date=9 May 2010|archive-date=16 July 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716094229/http://collections.si.edu/search/results.jsp?view=&date.slider=&fq=online_media_type:%22Sound+recordings%22&fq=online_visual_material:true&q=Harrington,&dsort=&fq=language:%22Chimariko%22|url-status=dead}} George Grekoff collected previous works of linguistics intending to write a grammar, but died before it was completed. The last Chimariko speaker was Martha Ziegler, who died in the 1950s. According to Golla, bilingual Hupa-Chimariko speakers native to the South Fork of the Trinity River, Burnt Ranch and New Rivers areas, organized as the [[Tsnungwe]] Tribe, "[are] seeking federal acknowledgement, consider both Hupa and Chimariko to be their heritage languages but emphasize Hupa for purposes of cultural revitalization." [[Low vowel|Low]] | || {{IPA link|a}} || |} === Syllables === Chimariko shares syllabic similarities with other languages in Northern California. The most common syllable structures for Chimariko are CV and CVC, with the largest possible structures being CCVC or CVCC.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b}} ==Grammar== Because the documentary corpus of Chimariko was limited, the description of the grammar of the language was not complete. However, general observations were made. Among the recorded grammatical characteristics are the following: Chimariko had [[reduplication]] in many nominal forms, particularly in the names of [[fauna]] (e.g., ''tsokoko-tci'' "bluejay", ''himimitcei'' "grouse"). Like many American languages (such as [[Shasta language|Shasta]], [[Maidu language|Maidu]], [[Wintu language|Wintun]], as well as [[Shoshoni language|Shoshoni]], [[Siouan]], and [[Pomo languages|Pomo]]), Chimariko verbs had a series of [[Instrumental case|instrumental]] and body-part [[prefix]]es, indicating the particular body part or object with which an action was carried out. Instrumentals are attached at the beginning of the verb root and often occur with a suffix which indicates the motion in the verb, such as {{lang|cid|-ha}} "up", {{lang|cid|-hot}} "down", and {{lang|cid|-usam}} "through".{{Harvnb|Dixon|1910}} {| class="wikitable" |+ List of instrumentals from Dixon: |- | {{lang|cid|a-}} || with a long object |- | {{lang|cid|e-}} || with the end of a long object |- | {{lang|cid|me-}} || with the head |- | {{lang|cid|mitci-}} || with the foot |- | {{lang|cid|tcu-}} || with a round object |- | {{lang|cid|tu-}} || with the hand |- | {{lang|cid|wa-}} || by sitting on |} Chimariko does not use numeral classifiers.{{Harvnb|Conathan|2004|p=11}} Also lacking is a clear pattern to indicate control.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b}} {| class="wikitable" |+ Pronominal affixes by verb stem class |- ! colspan="3" | 3rd person | {{lang|cid|hi}} || {{lang|cid|ha}} || {{lang|cid|he}} || {{lang|cid|ho}} || {{lang|cid|hu}} |}{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=69}} ===Morphology=== Noun incorporation is present in Chimariko.{{Harvnb|Mithun|1999|p=44}} The verbs have prefixes, suffixes and a circumfix.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=185}} Verb templates: {| class="wikitable" |- | Person || Root || Negative ''kuna'' || Directional || Tense/Aspect || Mood |} {| class="wikitable" |- | Person || Negative {{lang|cid|x-}} || Root || Negative {{lang|cid|-na}} || Directional || Tense/Aspect || Mood |} {| class="wikitable" |- | Root || Person || Tense/Aspect || Mood |} ===Numerals=== According to Carmen Jany, "no other language has the exact same system as Chimariko".{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=114}} Chimariko uses both a [[decimal]] and [[quinary]] numeral systems. Numerals appear in noun phrases, do not take affixes (except for the determinative suffix {{lang|cid|-lle}}), can either follow or precede the noun, and can appear without a noun.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|pp=112-113}} ===Space, time, modality=== There are two demonstrative pronouns in Chimariko indicating "here" and "there". {{lang|cid|Qè-}} indicates here, or near the speaker, and {{lang|cid|pa-}} indicates there, or a distance from the speaker. To indicate "this" and "that", the intensive suffix {{lang|cid|-ut}} is added: : This: {{lang|cid|qèwot}}, {{lang|cid|qât}} : That: {{lang|cid|pamut}}, {{lang|cid|paut}}, {{lang|cid|pât}} {| class="wikitable" |+ directional suffixes |- | {{lang|cid|-ktam/-tam}} || 'down' |- | {{lang|cid|-ema/-enak}} || 'into' |- | {{lang|cid|-ha}} || 'up' |- | {{lang|cid|-hot}} || 'down' |- | {{lang|cid|-lo}} || 'apart' |- | {{lang|cid|-ro}} || 'up' |- | {{lang|cid|-sku}} || 'towards' |- | {{lang|cid|-smu}} || 'across' |- | {{lang|cid|-tap}} || 'out' |- | {{lang|cid|-tku/-ku}} || Cislocative ('towards here') |- | {{lang|cid|-tmu/-mu}} || Transmotional ('towards there') |- | {{lang|cid|-kh}} || 'motion towards here' |- | {{lang|cid|-m}} || 'motion towards there' |- | {{lang|cid|-tpi}} || 'out of' |- | {{lang|cid|-xun/-xunok}} || 'in, into' |- | {{lang|cid|-qʰa}} || 'along' |- | {{lang|cid|-pa}} || 'off, away' |- | {{lang|cid|-qʰutu}} || 'into water' |- | {{lang|cid|-čʼana}} || 'to, toward' |- | {{lang|cid|-čama}} ||'in, into' |}{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|pp=247-248}} The modal system in Chimariko is abundant.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=206}} Modal suffixes attach at the very end of a verb after all other suffixes are applied and generally do not occur with aspectual suffixes. The modal suffixes function as interrogatives, negatives, dubitatives, speculatives, conditionals, emphatics, potentials, potential futures, purposive futures, optatives, desideratives, imperatives, admonitives, intensives, inferentials, resultatives, and evidentials.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|pp=206-209}} ===Sentence structure=== The research available indicates a variation in opinion about Chimariko's word order. Dixon claimed that usual word order is SVO or SOV, but in some cases the object precedes the subject, especially when the subject is pronominal. Jany claims that word order is not rigid but is mainly verb-final.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|pp=258-263}} The clauses are separated by brackets and the verbs are bolded in the following example: {{interlinear|lang=cid|number=ex:|glossing3=yes|italics2=yes |ʔawaidače xowonat, šičel hiwontat |[ʔawa-ida-če '''x-owo-na-t'''] [šičel '''h-iwonta-t'''] |home-POSS-LOC NEG-stay-NEG-ASP horse 3-ride-ASP |'She does not stay at home, she goes around on horseback.'{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=258}}}} Inside noun phrases, there is variation in order of modifiers and the noun; sometimes the noun comes before other elements of the phrase, sometimes after.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=264}} When dealing with possession, the subject always precedes the object.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=265}} ===Case=== Chimariko has an agent/patient case system.{{Harvnb|Mithun|1999|p=213}} For first persons, agent and patient are differentiated, and third persons are not.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007a|p=95}} Person hierarchy in the argument structure is present as well where speech act participants are favored over third persons.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=266}} {{interlinear|lang=cid|number=ex:|glossing3=yes|italics2=yes |mokoxanaˀ |'''m'''-oko-xana-ˀ |2SG-tattoo-FUT-Q |'Are you going to tattoo her?'{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b|p=270}} }} ===Possession=== Chimariko differentiates alienable and inalienable possession.{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b}} Alienable possessions such as objects and kinship are marked by suffix, while inalienable possessions such as body parts are marked by prefix, on the possessed. {| class="wikitable" |- ! colspan="3" | ! (complement is bolded; clauses are in brackets)}} '''Desiderative {{lang|cid|imiˀna}} ‘to want’ with clausal arguments''' {{interlinear|lang=cid|number=ex:|glossing3=yes|italics2=yes |yuwom imiˀnan |y-uwo-m imiˀna-n |1SG.A-go-DIR want-ASP |'I want to go home'}} ===Relative clauses=== In Chimariko, relativization can be done one of two ways – using a special verb suffix {{lang|cid|-rop/-rot}} to form internally headed clauses, and or by a headless relative clause. There is a relative pronoun {{lang|cid|map'un}} that is sometimes used. The following is an example given by Jany:{{Harvnb|Jany|2007b}} {{interlinear|lang=cid|number=ex:|glossing3=yes|italics2=yes |map’un hokoteˀrot yečiˀ ˀimiˀnan |['''map’un''' h-oko-teˀ-'''rot'''] y-ečiˀ ˀi-miˀn-an |that.one 3-?-DER-DEP 1SG.A-buy 1SG-want-ASP |I want to buy that engraved one.}} The relative clause is in brackets. {{lang|cid|map’un}} is the head. ==Vocabulary== ===Placenames=== This table lists a few present-day locations in Chimariko territory.{{cite web | url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ufj4HiW9HbtP6a-v-WJOyXTneBQxekaM/view | title=Chimariko Place Names: Toponymy and Geolinguistics | publisher=Chimariko Language | accessdate=November 20, 2022}} :{| class="wikitable sortable" !
